chapters.caption: Tower Bridge from the south bank — steel frame dressed in Cornish granite and Portland stone
chapters.directions: The Exhibition entrance is in the North Tower, on the Tower of London side. Head inside and take the lift (or the 206 steps) up.
chapters.text: First, the correction everyone needs: this is Tower Bridge — not London Bridge. London Bridge is the rather plain crossing half a mile upstream; this Gothic fairytale is the one on the tea towels. And second surprise: it's not nearly as old as it looks. The bridge opened in 1894, making it a contemporary of the Eiffel Tower, and underneath that medieval-looking stone cladding is a thoroughly modern Victorian steel frame. So why did London build it? By the 1870s, the East End had exploded with docks and warehouses, and the river crossings couldn't cope — but any new bridge had to let tall-masted ships through to the Pool of London, the busy port just upstream. Parliament demanded a design that worked for road traffic and river traffic at once, and after years of wrangling — over 50 designs were submitted, including one with a huge rotating platform — the city chose a bascule bridge: from the French for 'seesaw.' The two roadways in the middle pivot up like drawbridges, counterweighted, so a ship can pass. Architect Horace Jones and engineer John Wolfe Barry gave it its famous disguise: stone towers in the Gothic style, chosen specifically to harmonise with the Tower of London next door. Eight years of construction, five major contractors, more than 400 workers, and 11,000 tons of steel went into it. Stand back before you go in and admire the trick: a machine, dressed as a castle.
chapters.title: Why This Bridge Exists — The Problem It Solved

chapters.caption: Inside the North Tower — construction photos, divers' suits and the builders' stories
chapters.directions: Ride the lift to the top of the North Tower for the walkways. The West Walkway comes first.
chapters.text: As you climb the North Tower — and do take the stairs if your knees allow, because the stairwells double as exhibition space — the bridge introduces you to the people who built it. Look for the photographs: workmen perched on steel beams high over the river, in flat caps, with no harnesses worth mentioning. Building this bridge was genuinely dangerous work. The towers stand on piers sunk into the riverbed, and to dig those foundations, men worked in caissons — huge iron boxes on the river bottom — in compressed air, an environment that could give you the bends. Divers in standard dress, those brass-helmeted suits that look like something from Jules Verne, worked on the riverbed in near darkness; one of those immensely heavy suits is on display, and standing next to it makes the job feel very real. You'll also see the rejected designs — London could have had a very different bridge — and portraits and plaques honouring the ordinary workers, an unusually democratic touch for a Victorian monument. My favourite small detail from the displays: cats once lived in the engine rooms, officially, to keep the rodent population down among the machinery. Every great monument has its unsung staff. Here, some of them were cats.
chapters.title: Climbing the North Tower — The Builders

chapters.caption: The West Walkway, 42 metres above the Thames
chapters.directions: Cross the West Walkway to the South Tower, pausing at the glass floor section. Then continue to the East Walkway for the downstream view.
chapters.text: Now step out onto the high-level walkways, 42 metres — 138 feet — above the river. Here's a bit of history most visitors miss: these walkways weren't built as a tourist attraction. They were a practical necessity. When the bascules rise for a ship, road traffic stops — but pedestrians were supposed to climb up here and cross over the top, so the bridge never fully closed to foot traffic. The public, being sensible, mostly preferred to wait downstairs rather than climb hundreds of steps, and pickpockets loved the quiet walkways, so they were closed in 1910 and stayed shut for over 70 years, reopening only in 1982 as part of the exhibition. Lucky us, because the views are superb and the perspective is unique in London: you're not on a skyscraper looking down at the city, you're in the middle of the river, at ship height, with the Thames running away in both directions. Take your time crossing. The walkway windows include some that open, which photographers love — no glass glare between you and the shot. And if the bridge lifts while you're up here — it still opens around 800 times a year — you'll feel the whole structure hum faintly with machinery. That's not a fault. That's the building doing its day job.
chapters.title: The High-Level Walkways — A Victorian Commuter Shortcut

chapters.caption: The glass floor — road and river, 42 metres straight down
chapters.directions: Continue across to the South Tower and take the lift or stairs down. Follow the blue line painted on the pavement outside to the Engine Rooms entrance, under the southern approach.
chapters.text: Deep breath. In 2014, sections of the walkway floors were replaced with glass panels — 11 metres long, each panel weighing over 500 kilos and built from layers that could hold the weight of an elephant or two London taxis, in case you're worried. Step out onto the glass and look straight down: buses, black cabs, cyclists and pedestrians stream across the bridge deck far below, and the Thames slides past on either side. It is genuinely vertiginous for the first few seconds, and then — for most people — genuinely fun. If you're lucky enough to be standing here during a bridge lift, you'll watch the bascules rise beneath you, which is the single best seat in London for it; the bridge lift times are published in advance, and timing your visit for one is the pro move. Practical reassurance: there's a solid floor running right alongside the glass, so nobody has to step onto it — plenty of visitors cross on the solid strip, and that's fine. But do try at least standing with one foot on it. And look up in the West Walkway: there's a mirrored ceiling above the glass floor, installed so you can take a photo of yourself apparently floating over the river. Silly? Absolutely. Worth it? Also absolutely.
chapters.title: The Glass Floor — Look Down, If You Dare

chapters.caption: Upstream from the walkway: the Tower, HMS Belfast, the City and the Shard
chapters.directions: From the South Tower, the blue line leads you under the bridge's southern approach road to the Victorian Engine Rooms.
chapters.text: Before you head down, use the walkways as what they really are: a free orientation lecture on London. Face upstream, to the west, and read the city left to right. Closest, on the north bank, is the Tower of London — if you've just come from there, this is your victory lap view: the White Tower, the walls, the green moat, all laid out like a model. Moored in the river is HMS Belfast, the Royal Navy cruiser that fired some of the first shots on D-Day and is now a museum ship. Behind it rises the City of London, the financial district, with its cluster of nicknamed towers — the Walkie-Talkie, the Cheesegrater, the Gherkin — and, in the distance, the dome of St Paul's Cathedral, which still anchors every London panorama. Turn around and look downstream, east: the river bends away toward Canary Wharf's towers and, eventually, Greenwich and the sea — this was the working river, the greatest port in the world in the bridge's heyday, and the reason the bascules exist. On the south bank below you is the Shard, western Europe's tallest building when it opened, and the old wharves of Bermondsey now converted into flats and restaurants. Two directions, two Londons: the ancient port looking east, the money looking west. This bridge stands exactly on the seam between them, which is really the story of the whole city.
chapters.title: The Views — Reading London from the River

chapters.caption: The Victorian Engine Rooms — the original steam engines that lifted the bridge until 1976
chapters.directions: The Engine Rooms are the last section of the Exhibition. Exit back to the south bank pavement — the Thames Path west takes you toward the Shard and Borough Market; east takes you back toward the Tower.
chapters.text: Follow the blue line on the pavement down to the south side, and step into the bridge's engine rooms — for my money, the most underrated part of the whole visit. These cavernous rooms under the southern approach hold the original Victorian machinery: enormous steam pumping engines, coal-fired boilers, and the great hydraulic accumulators, all polished and painted in green and red like showpieces. Here's how it worked. The steam engines pumped water into the accumulators — towering cylinders with massive weights on top — storing energy as pressurised water, at about 750 pounds per square inch. When a ship approached, that stored pressure was released to drive the machinery that swings each bascule up: over 1,000 tons of roadway and steel, lifted to 83 degrees in about a minute. Storing the power in advance was the genius of the system — the bridge didn't have to wait for steam to build; the energy was always sitting there, ready. This hydraulic system, cutting-edge in 1894, ran the bridge until 1976, when it was replaced by electric and oil-hydraulic machinery — look for the modern control room displays too. But the steam engines were kept, lovingly, and standing among them you understand the bridge differently: not as a picture postcard, but as a power station with a road on top.
chapters.title: The Victorian Engine Rooms — Steam, Pressure, and Genius

chapters.caption: Tower Bridge at dusk — still a working bridge, lifting around 800 times a year
chapters.directions: You're done! From the south bank, St Katharine Docks and the Tower are a short walk back across the bridge at road level — crossing on foot is free, as it always has been.
chapters.text: Here's the thought to take away with you: Tower Bridge is not a ruin, a replica, or a museum piece that happens to look like a bridge. It's a working machine that has lifted for river traffic continuously since 1894 — around 800 lifts a year, 24 hours a day, with river traffic still having right of way over road traffic, by law. Ships give 24 hours' notice, the bridge team swings into action, and London's traffic simply waits, as it has for 130 years. If you have any flexibility in your day, check the published lift times and try to watch one from the riverbank — the sight of that roadway rearing up, and a tall ship gliding through the middle of a London street, never gets old. And if you're here at dusk, stay a little longer: the bridge is beautifully lit after dark, and the walk back across at road level, with the Tower floodlit on one side and the river glittering on the other, is one of the great free experiences in London. From here, the south bank is your oyster — wander west along the Thames Path toward the Shard, Borough Market, and the Globe, or cross back north for the Tower and the City. Thanks for climbing up with me — most people only photograph this bridge. You've been inside the machine.
chapters.title: Wrap-Up — Still a Working Bridge

intro: Everyone photographs Tower Bridge; far fewer people go inside it. That's a shame, because the inside is where the story is: a Victorian steam-powered machine dressed up as a medieval castle, with walkways 42 metres above the Thames and a glass floor that lets you watch London traffic stream beneath your feet. The Exhibition takes you up the North Tower, across both high-level walkways, and down into the original Engine Rooms on the south bank. Allow about 75 minutes — and if you can, time your visit to a scheduled bridge lift, when the roadways rise for a passing ship. Let's climb.
mapNote: The Exhibition route is one-way and easy to follow. You enter at the North Tower (the Tower of London side), ride or climb to the top, and cross to the South Tower via the West Walkway (upstream views, glass floor). From the South Tower you can return along the East Walkway (downstream views) within the towers' exhibition level. Then you descend the South Tower, step outside, and follow the blue line painted on the pavement under the southern approach to the Victorian Engine Rooms — the final section. Exiting the Engine Rooms puts you on the south bank. Crossing the bridge at road level, on foot, is always free and separate from the Exhibition.
practical: One ticket covers everything: both towers, the walkways and glass floors, and the Victorian Engine Rooms. You don't need separate tickets for the Engine Rooms.
Check the bridge lift schedule before you visit (published on the Tower Bridge website) and time your entry so you're on the walkways during a lift — it's the highlight of the whole experience.
Allow 60–90 minutes. The Engine Rooms are a separate section on the south bank at the end, and visitors who rush the towers often skip them — don't.
The glass floor has a solid walkway alongside it the whole way, so anyone nervous about heights can cross comfortably and still enjoy the views.
Take the stairs in the North Tower if you can: the stairwell displays on the builders and divers are part of the exhibition. Lifts are available for step-free access.
Photography is allowed throughout, and some walkway windows open for glare-free shots — the best Tower of London photo in the city is from up here.
Crossing the bridge at street level is free; if you're short on time, even a walk across gives you the river views and the bascules up close.
subtitle: Inside London's most famous bridge — walkways, glass floor, and steam engines
title: Tower Bridge
